title: Putin is far from isolated. Europe must play him at the long game
author: jon.wallace
description:
Putin is far from isolated. Europe must play him at the long game  Expert comment jon.wallace 15 September 2026

The SCO and BRICS summits indicate Russia retains sufficient value to China, India and other non-Western powers to pursue its war objectives. Europe needs to adjust to that reality.

The past fortnight has seen President Vladimir Putin undertake plenty of summit diplomacy. Throughout he has shown no sign he is open to compromise on Russia’s war aims in Ukraine. On the contrary, escalation has accelerated. 

Europe seems inclined to read this increased aggression as a sign of desperation on Moscow’s part. But that is a miscalculation. In reality, the Kremlin’s strategy of blended diplomatic impassivity and calibrated escalation may be stronger than it looks.

No backing down

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spent more than three hours with Putin in Moscow on 5 September, discussing how to end the war. The Kremlin hailed the discussions as ‘highly useful’ but gave no indication that it was ready to relax its demands: Ukrainian territorial concessions and restrictions on Kyiv’s future security alignment. Days later, an offer by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet Putin at December’s G20 summit in Miami was rebuffed.

Meanwhile, Russian attacks have intensified. On 13 September, a Russian drone struck railway infrastructure near Yahodyn, shortly after a train carrying Boris Johnson, former CIA director David Petraeus and others had passed through the area. Whether they were deliberately targeted remains unknown. What is certain is that the strike was part of Russia’s largest drone barrage in months and followed intensified attacks on Ukrainian transport, energy and civilian infrastructure.

Many European officials argue that Moscow’s behaviour shows it is running out of options in Ukraine. Indeed, Russia’s position is uncertain. It is suffering extraordinary losses. Its territorial advances remain slow and costly. And Ukrainian forces have regained ground in several sectors. 

Yet the conclusion that Russian escalation betrays desperation is closer to wishful thinking than reality. Putin behaves like someone who still believes time is on his side and that he retains room for manoeuvre. His recent diplomacy offers a useful interpretative framework.

Putin can (still) afford to ignore friendly advice

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s July intervention on the Ukraine war rightfully attracted considerable attention. Sitting alongside Putin in Omsk, Tokayev said the conflict should be frozen and negotiations resumed. The Kremlin promptly rejected the idea of a freeze.

Narendra Modi went a step further in Bishkek on 31 August, at the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), telling Putin publicly that the world needed to ‘move from endless war to end of war’. Yet Modi also addressed Putin as his ‘friend’, praised the strength of Russia–India relations and less than two weeks later, during the BRICS summit, discussed a bilateral trade target of $100 billion with Putin. 

There is no reason to doubt that governments like India and Kazakhstan genuinely want the war to end. But that does not mean they are prepared to make their relations with Russia conditional upon it. 

This distinction explains much of Putin’s confidence. Despite its criticism, India continues to treat Russia as a key strategic partner. And, while Kazakhstan has carefully diversified its foreign relations, it has preserved a close relationship with Moscow. Meanwhile the New Delhi BRICS declaration criticised unilateral sanctions and trade restrictions while avoiding directly confronting Russia over Ukraine. 

These sustained partnerships may provide Moscow with something it needs almost as critically as support for the war in Ukraine: economic integration in Asia, diplomatic legitimacy, and a respected role in influential international groupings.

Russia is valuable to China too

Chinese President Xi Jinping told Putin at the SCO summit that the foundations of their bilateral relationship would only become stronger.

Russia is often described by Europeans as China’s ‘vassal’. This captures a genuine economic asymmetry: China’s economy is roughly eight times larger than Russia’s. And Russia conducts at least 34 per cent of its international trade with China, whereas Russia accounts for only around 4 per cent of China’s.  

But it is missing an important aspect of the partnership, which cannot be measured through bilateral trade alone. Beijing has reasons to keep Moscow strong enough to remain an independent power. Russia has a nuclear arsenal, a permanent UN Security Council seat, vast energy and commodity resources, and a strategic position straddling Central Asia and the Arctic. Most importantly, Moscow is willing to challenge what remains of the US-shaped world order. 

Chinese involvement in Russia’s war economy shows that the relationship is more consistent than many in Europe may think. 

Documents reported this month by Politico suggest that a Chinese state-owned firm shipped carbon fibre used in Geran attack drones to Alabuga-Volokno, a sanctioned subsidiary of Rosatom (Russia’s state-owned nuclear conglomerate). An earlier investigation by the Robert Lansing Institute documented Chinese engines and components in Russian drones. Last year, Reuters reported that Chinese drone specialists were working with Russian manufacturers.

This does not prove that every transaction was ordered by Beijing. Nor is it evidence of ‘limitless’ Chinese support. Xi has no interest in becoming hostage to Putin’s decisions and Beijing will continue to calibrate its exposure very carefully. It does show, however, how misleading it is to equate China’s rhetorical caution over Ukraine with distance from Russia.

For Beijing, Moscow remains the useful disruptor-in-chief. Its actions help an alternative international system emerge, through groups like the SCO and BRICS, in which US and European power carry less weight. And even though these groups’ members disagree profoundly about what a more multipolar order should look like, they offer increasingly clear diplomatic expression to China’s ambition. 

India may not share China’s vision of global order, but neither does it see an advantage in isolating Russia. Nor does Kazakhstan or any other BRICS member. This has proved a comfortable enough ambiguity with which Putin has learned to live.

More realism is needed in Europe

These past few months of Russian escalation against Ukraine and Europe, and diplomatic consolidation with Asia, should teach European leaders a lesson: Their effort to shame governments into choosing between Russia and the West has clearly reached its limits – if not failed.

The European Union (EU)’s relations with India may offer a better model. This has seen the EU strengthen commercial ties with India while lowering its tone over New Delhi’s relationship with Moscow.

The World Today

Related work

The Open Centre: Reimagining Europe’s offer to a fractured world

This makes sense: there is considerable scope to deepen relations with India and Central Asia. Europe can offer investment, technology, access to the single market, and critical-mineral partnerships. It can also offer transport routes that reduce dependence on Russia, such as the Trans-Caspian corridor. 

By using such an approach, Europe can adjust to a new reality, working patiently to widen the space between Russia and its partners rather than assume that the separation is already underway. 

On China, the EU has already sanctioned a growing number of Chinese companies involved in sanctions circumvention and Russia’s military-industrial complex. 

The success of Europe’s own long game may hinge on how far the EU is prepared to extend those sanctions and hit strategic supply chains when the evidence points to direct involvement by larger or state-owned Chinese suppliers. 

Russia’s escalation in Ukraine indicates that Putin still wagers he can outlast Ukraine’s supporters. He remains confident that Russia is sufficiently connected to the rest of the world to absorb Western pressure. And he sees his position as bolstered by what he believes is a US weakened by war with Iran. Putin’s summit diplomacy of the past few months suggests that, at least for now, he has some reason to be confident.

But Europe does not have to accept his wager. What it must do is understand the underlying long-term dynamics and respond accordingly. If Putin is playing the long game, perhaps it is time Europe does too.

title: What can DRC’s national dialogue achieve?
author: jon.wallace
description:
What can DRC’s national dialogue achieve? Expert comment jon.wallace 24 September 2026

President Tshisekedi and the opposition both want national dialogue. But it remains to be seen whether they can agree on the nature of the DRC’s problems, let alone their solutions.

When President of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) Félix Tshisekedi finally announced a ‘national dialogue’ on 27 August, he evoked the country’s long history of previous negotiations. Too often, he said, they had been about elite power sharing, had not meaningfully included the Congolese people, and had legitimized armed insurrection. This time will be different, he promised.

Tshisekedi appealed directly to the Congolese people by proposing a series of public consultations in all 26 provinces, culminating in a convention in Kinshasa. Unlike previous dialogues, this process has a more ambitious aim. It not only seeks to address the causes of insecurity and inequality in DRC and identify reforms. It also seeks to reconstruct or re-found the state.

The opposition immediately denounced the project. The C64, a coalition made up of opposition heavyweights including Moïse Katumbi, Martin Fayulu, Delly Sesanga and Jean-Marc Kabund, rejected Tshisekedi’s proposal. So too did the ‘Sauvons le Congo’ platform created by exiled former president Joseph Kabila.

Tshisekedi’s plan, they claim, is intended above all to legitimize his attempt to change the constitution, possibly allowing the president to extend his rule beyond his two-term limit, which ends in 2028. They point to a controversial bill that would pave the way for a referendum allowing the modification of article 220 of the constitution, which forbids changing the number or duration of presidential terms.

Points of (dis)agreement

There is much that the DRC’s government and opposition disagree on. But there are two points of convergence. One, publicly acknowledged, is the need for a national dialogue to address the country’s serious challenges. However, apart from the need to bring peace to the eastern provinces, there is no consensus on what these challenges are.

The other point of convergence, acknowledged only behind closed doors, is that elections probably cannot be held by the end of Tshisekedi’s second term in 2028. There are three main reasons: First, little progress has been made in organizing them. Technically there is still time to do so, but the quality of elections held in 2028 would be in question. 

Second, important territories in eastern DRC remain captured by the M23 armed group. Any attempt to exclude these provinces from elections could be interpreted as an implicit endorsement of their secession, raising fears of the break-up of the country. Third, some members of the opposition may see a dialogue as a way to gain power without going to the polls.

There is therefore broad, albeit tacit, agreement on the need to delay elections in favour of ‘dialogue’. But consensus falls apart when talk of detail begins. Indeed, it raises the question: what dialogue is needed to resolve which crisis?

For Tshisekedi, the national dialogue is an opportunity to create a ‘united front’ – under his control – aligned against Rwanda. In the president’s telling, the DRC’s problems stem mainly from Rwanda’s support for the M23 in North and South Kivu provinces. Since late 2021, M23 fighters have seized large swathes of territory, including the provincial capitals of Goma and Bukavu. Tshisekedi has dismissed opposition calls to integrate M23 in the national dialogue, saying the Doha Process – Qatar-led talks hosted in Switzerland – is the only appropriate venue for negotiating with them.

But for many in the opposition, as well as the Catholic and Protestant churches, the conflict is more a symptom of the political crisis than its cause. In their view, the M23’s success has been fuelled by dissatisfaction with bad governance and corruption under Tshisekedi’s government.

Many want a neutral convenor for a dialogue, such as the churches, and a venue outside of the DRC that would allow exiled politicians to participate. But Tshisekedi has ruled out an external location. And he has made clear that religious denominations will play a secondary or even symbolic role.

What a post-2028 transition might look like, if elections are not held, is still open for debate. The concept recalls the two-year ‘glissement’ (literally, ‘sliding’) that former president Joseph Kabila negotiated to remain in power beyond the end of this second term, in 2016-17.

For those close to President Tshisekedi, there is hope of getting broad agreement on a transition that could last three to five years. That would be a de facto extension of the president’s tenure beyond constitutional limits, if he remained in office for the duration. Some in the opposition would like to see a shorter transition, even without Tshisekedi. This would see a power-sharing agreement that would pave the way for a new electoral commission and fresh elections.

However, for now the country’s opposition seems fragmented and unable to shape the terms of the dialogue. Crucially, they lack the leverage of significant popular mobilization: a long-postponed opposition rally on 15 September saw relatively little participation on the streets of the capital. And the US, which recently signed a critical minerals deal with the DRC, is seen to be backing Tshisekedi. The president therefore seems likely to move forward with his plan. A recent presidential ordinance laid the groundwork for the dialogue proceeding under Tshisekedi’s control.

The position of the Catholic and Protestant churches may yet prove influential. For the moment, they have not commented publicly, preferring to try to negotiate for a stronger role. However, should their position change and church leaders choose to actively boycott the dialogue, it could diminish the legitimacy of the process. The Catholic church is an important political actor in the DRC: it was instrumental in organizing against a Kabila third term. For now, however, Tshisekedi appears to have the stronger hand.  

It may be that Tshisekedi’s stated goal of going beyond past national dialogues to ‘re-found’ the state is just political rhetoric. The risk is that he intends to use talks as a way of co-opting part of the opposition, just as Kabila did in 2016-17.

Related work

Africa Aware: DRC’s Ebola outbreak: Local systems, international responses and lessons for Africa

Meanwhile the opposition wants to wrest power from Tshisekedi but also does not necessarily favour elections to resolve the political crisis. It may therefore view dialogue as the best means of unseating the president and taking power. Either way, the two sides’ framings are fundamentally at odds. It remains to be seen whether all parties can agree on the nature of the nation’s problems, let alone their solutions.

The debate over the dialogue is a reminder that the security situation in the east cannot be neatly separated from national politics. Talk of changing the constitution by Tshisekedi’s camp waned in early 2025, after the M23 seized Goma and Bukavu. It resurged once the threat was contained.

Fundamentally linked 

The current assemblage of processes – Washington for DRC–Rwanda negotiations, the Doha process for DRC–M23 talks and now, the national dialogue – draw lines between phenomena and actors that are fundamentally linked.

The relatively limited objectives of the Washington and Doha processes are at least clearer than the national dialogue’s ambiguous aim of ‘re-founding’ the Congolese state or ‘creating peace’. But each process’s success is linked to the other. No agreement with the M23 can exist without an accord with Rwanda. And peace in the east will require progress on transitional justice and community reconciliation – issues which should be part of any national dialogue.

Can a national dialogue deliver the reforms DRC desperately needs? Currently, the greatest risk is that it is limited in exactly the way Tshisekedi said it must not be: to an exercise in which political elites agree how and when power will change hands.

title: Denmark’s Greenland deal with Trump is a victory for diplomacy over bullying
author: jon.wallace
description:
Denmark’s Greenland deal with Trump is a victory for diplomacy over bullying Expert comment jon.wallace 24 September 2026

Denmark used its soft power to rally support and took the dispute out of the limelight – addressing underlying US interests instead of President Trump’s unacceptable public position.

This week, Denmark has extricated itself from a period of coercive US diplomacy over Greenland. The agreement announced on 22 September elegantly resolves the dispute over the territory, without forcing Denmark or the government of Greenland to give up very much. 

Even before the dispute, Denmark had indicated it would be content to increase the number of US bases in Greenland and enhance US access to them. These measures were already possible under an existing 1951 agreement. 

The new agreement adds an undertaking by Denmark and Greenland to refuse major investments from non-members of the EU or NATO that would grant them a foothold in strategic Arctic areas. Again, on this point, Washington was pushing on an open door.

The only meaningful change concerns the mechanism to ensure that this arrangement will be permanent. The 1951 agreement, amended in 2004, also does not expire. But the new text adds that Greenland will remain part of NATO and continue to comply with the agreement, should it opt for independence. 

An independent Greenland might have been willing to retain the US bases and related agreements anyway. After all, it would need to rely on US defence support and a NATO security guarantee. But expressly making these points in an agreement co-signed by Greenland overcame the deal-breaker of President Donald Trump’s demand for sovereignty over all of Greenland or at least the US base areas.

The agreement represents a masterclass by Denmark in using the classical art of diplomacy to overcome bullying, in an age of changing geopolitics and unstable global governance. 

Indeed, the steps Denmark took to resolve the dispute provide valuable insight into how countries can defend their interests in the face of apparently overwhelming pressure.

Step 1: Isolate the bully and call the game

In January this year, President Trump declared that the US would need to ‘own’ Greenland to prevent Russia or China from taking it, and to ensure US national security. He even raised the option of a military takeover of the territory.

The president may have believed opposition would be minimal. Just days before, EU and NATO countries had been unwilling to confront him publicly over the armed US intervention against Venezuela, despite it being a clear breach of international law. In the emergency meeting of the UN Security Council that followed, they had stayed meekly silent. 

Greenland was different. Denmark could clearly assert that Trump was placing the future of NATO in peril. Hence, Denmark could show that the US action posed a threat to both the territorial integrity of Denmark and to the security of all states in Western Europe. Accordingly, NATO countries and EU members overcame their hesitancy to upset the White House, and strongly and unanimously rejected his demand. Indeed, they went further, dispatching a European defence mission to Greenland, supposedly as a matter of routine.

Calling out the US’s game for what it was – a demand to surrender national territory under the threat of force at a time when the West was resisting Putin’s assault on Ukraine – was crucial in rallying support.

Step 2: Enter the fray with clean hands

In this dispute, Denmark continually had the advantage in the battle for international sympathy. It entered the fray with clean hands, taking advantage of its soft power, which has been nurtured over decades of sensitive advocacy for justice in relation to the Global South and the international rule of law. The US under Trump, on the other hand, has caused continued upset throughout, as a result of its military actions and other activity such as the president’s sweeping ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs.

Learn more about our Global Governance and Security Centre

The Centre provides analysis and problem-solving to improve global governance in a fracturing world order.

The US could also not accuse Denmark of hypocrisy over any supposed colonial legacy relating to Greenland. By 1954, the UN General Assembly had determined that Greenland had freely decided to integrate with Denmark on the basis of equal constitutional and administrative standing with other parts of Denmark. 

By 1979 Copenhagen offered home rule. Two decades later, in 2009, it granted wide-ranging self-government to Greenland. Crucially, this 2009 arrangement included an express right of self-determination for the people of Greenland, with a provision to opt for independence. Any sale of Greenland (as Trump had previously proposed) or its transfer to the US against the wishes of the population, would have violated this existing right to self-determination. 

This meant that throughout the dispute, Denmark could claim a role as both the upholder of the international right to self-determination, and the defender of its own territorial integrity.

Step 3: Clarify the legal status

President Trump sought to enhance his claim by suggesting that Denmark did not have a clear title to Greenland. In view of the 2009 agreement’s self-determination provisions, this assertion became less relevant. In any event, it was easy to prove that Denmark held good title. And the US clearly had none at all. 

In 1916 US Secretary of State Robert Lansing issued a declaration accepting Denmark’s claim to the island. When the US took over the defence of Greenland during Germany’s occupation of Denmark during the Second World War, it did so in ‘recognition and respect for the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Denmark over Greenland.’ 

This expressly included Danish sovereignty over base areas constructed by the US. The post-war agreements on defence cooperation and US bases of 1951 and 2004 also consistently confirmed Danish sovereignty. Indeed, in an amazing reversal of the US position, so does the new 2026 agreement. The text reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Denmark and acknowledges Greenland’s right to self-determination. 

Step 4: Dial the temperature down and let experts do the work

When encountering the US, Denmark was careful to avoid a public confrontation with Trump in front of cameras, learning from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s experience at the Oval Office in 2025. 

Instead, when the row intensified, Copenhagen dispatched Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen to Washington. As foreign minister, protocol demanded that he should meet with the slightly more moderate US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, instead of the president. 

Vice President JD Vance almost derailed this cunning plan when he insisted on leading the meeting and moving it to the White House. But Rasmussen, a former Danish prime minister, calmly focused on shared security interests in the Arctic. And he remained steadfast where sovereignty and the rights of Greenlanders were concerned.

After a supposed breakthrough on the issue at the Davos conference later in January 2026, Denmark managed to divert dialogue to technical meetings, held confidentially, outside of the public eye. This was the critical change that allowed Copenhagen to defang the entire episode.

Step 5: Focus on interests, not positions

Negotiations experts know that success depends on persuading the sides to step away from their incompatible, publicly stated position and instead address their underlying interests. In this instance, President Trump had claimed that only full sovereignty over Greenland would answer US security needs. 

At Davos, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte offered the US sovereignty at least over its base areas in Greenland. Trump seized that initiative and accepted, withdrawing his threat of invasion. 

However, neither Denmark nor Greenland representatives had been party to that proposal. Handing over even a part of sovereign territory would hardly be acceptable to their parliaments.

But in the technical discussions, it became possible to move from a flat-out demand for sovereignty, to achieving the underlying US desire: a permanent arrangement safeguarding its interests in Greenland. 

Step 6: Be generous in victory

On signing the agreement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was careful to avoid any sense of climb-down by President Trump. It is a deal that can ‘last forever,’ she said, reflecting Trump’s claim that he had achieved an outcome just as permanent as a transfer of sovereignty.

As President Trump’s original stated position was that ‘the ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity’, this new agreement seems a clear victory for calm and quiet Danish diplomacy. And it plainly illustrates the power of unity among NATO states and EU members. The lessons for future dealings with great powers are clear.

title: US voters are angry. But on tariffs and war, the midterms won’t bring quick change
author: LToremark
description:
US voters are angry. But on tariffs and war, the midterms won’t bring quick change Expert comment LToremark 22 October 2026

Despite their anger, American voters are unlikely to see much immediate change to the international policies that are driving up costs at home: tariffs and the Iran war.

As the US midterms approach, American voters are angry. They are angry about the economy, about prices and about insecurity. And they have connected their plight at home with the Trump administration’s international policies.

Public opinion directly connects tariffs to high prices.  An August survey found that 75 per cent of Americans worry about being able to afford groceries and goods, while 83 per cent of those worried say tariffs have increased the prices of those goods. And as many as three in four voters say tariffs will influence their vote.

Voters are also angry about the Iran war, which they directly connect to the cost of living. Majorities say that even if Trump ended the war before the midterms, they would not view his party more favourably.

Related work

Why the US midterms are a rare foreign policy election

The last time midterm voters were this angry about international issues was in 2006, as the Iraq war turned sour. But after that election, then-president George W Bush adopted even more aggressive policies in Iraq, the so-called ‘surge’ of 2007. Trump’s public statements suggest that he, too, is likely to be more aggressive on both war and tariffs. His political style explains some of this, but so does the extent to which the executive branch holds power over international policies. 

Democrats have said if they win one or both houses of Congress they will initiate investigations into corruption and the rule of law. But efforts to claw back power will be slow – and even slower to yield results in voters’ wallets.

Changing course on Iran?

On the war with Iran, all the factors that have prevented a deal before the midterm elections will still be in place after 3 November. Voices from the region and the US alike are speculating whether there will be renewed conflict after the midterms and forecasting different ways in which the war could be expanded, from an assault on Iran’s nuclear facilities to a more aggressive proxy war waged from Iraq. Meanwhile, Trump has announced that 9,000 additional troops are being sent to the region.

Some members of Congress are already looking at the tools they have to force an end to the war. One such tool is the War Powers Act of 1973, which requires congressional approval for any hostilities lasting longer than 60 days. Such a resolution has already passed the House of Representatives three times, with the support of a few Republicans. Trump has thus far managed to prevent it from being passed by the Senate, most recently only by one vote. It is not much of a stretch to imagine the resolution passing both houses in the next Congress. 

However, previous congressional attempts to use it have been vetoed and ignored by presidents of both parties – including Trump in 2019 (Yemen) and again in 2020 (Iran). Courts have also declined hearing cases brought by members of Congress seeking to enforce the Act, saying they lacked jurisdiction while legislative remedies were available. Passage of a joint resolution will up the political pressure on Trump but nothing more.  

That leaves Congress with its other tool – the power of the purse. When the current Congress returns shortly after the elections for a so-called ‘lame duck’ session before the newly elected Congress is seated in January, it will be asked to vote on the Pentagon’s request for extra money to fund the Iran war. Democrats and a few Republicans have already blocked such funding from being passed once, and a lively public battle is sure to follow. However, while this would not be the first time a Congress has threatened to cut off funding for wars it disapproves of, it has never actually followed through on such threats. 

Sometimes though, the threat and public debate can be enough to have an impact. Congress – even in its current configuration – is unlikely to approve the $1.5 billion military budget Trump requested before the war with Iran, a 44 per cent increase. As the US military struggles to replace expensive missiles and meet its deterrence commitments elsewhere in the world, pressure will grow to end the war – or at least to dial it back to reduce costs. But that won’t be quick and it won’t be decisive enough to help lower prices, which is what American consumers say they are voting for. 

Doubling down on tariffs

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

On tariffs, the prospects appear more straightforward. The US Constitution reserves tariff power to Congress. Congressional majorities opposing the Trump tariffs could, if they wished, repeal them and set tariff levels in law, or explicitly bar the Trump administration from raising tariffs without congressional consent. 

But that is easier said than done. For the last decade, congresses of various partisan compositions have opposed both free trade agreements and tariffs proposed by presidents but have been unable to find trade policy that cross-partisan majorities can support. This is likely to continue. Congressional Democrats have previewed plans for ambitious investigations of corruption allegations in how Trump’s trade deals were negotiated, and how exemptions to tariffs are granted. But they disagree deeply about what ideal tariff levels should be and are sceptical of gaining enough Republican cooperation for broader tariff relief beyond specific sectors, such as school supplies or construction materials.

Meanwhile, far from bending to popular opinion and reducing tariffs, the Trump administration is doubling down. 

It has initiated another round of ‘section 301’ investigations into the EU and 15 other economies, alleging that they systematically overproduce in order to export at unfairly low prices. It has also left the door open to tariff action on semiconductors, critical minerals and commercial aircraft (and parts) under so-called ‘section 232’ allegations that trade conditions are harming US national security. 

Finally, it has launched a request for comment on how the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) impacts US businesses, including ‘whether and what enforcement action may be appropriate to remedy any negative effects’. Those comments are due the week after the midterms and open up a range of options, including a public hearing or a formal investigation. The Trump administration will therefore be able to use the threat or reality of CBAM tariffs next year; either as a negotiating tool or as a next round of tariffs should any of the current measures be overturned in court.

With the midterm results likely to put Trump under pressure to change unpopular policies, explicit voter anger will also put pressure on a new Congress to be more aggressive than in recent years, to use the power it does have over budgets and tariffs. Absent that, voters are likely to find that their vote was like pushing a lever that is not connected to anything. And that is likely to increase frustration even more – upping the chances for surprising results in the 2028 presidential election.

title: Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030?
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030? Expert comment thilton.drupal 22 October 2026

Egyptian president’s surprise announcement comes amid deep economic difficulties and includes a plan for a military-approved succession.

Egypt’s President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi has declared he will step down at the end of his third term in 2030. Speaking during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation on 17 October, he also outlined a military-centric succession process to select the next president and senior officials beyond 2030. 

The statement surprised many observers, and perhaps even state officials. If Sisi follows through on his pledge and leaves peacefully, he’d be the first Egyptian president to leave office without dying, being imprisoned or facing a popular uprising. 

The unprecedented decision will have significant implications for Egypt’s political landscape, the balance of power within the regime and the military’s influence over politics and governance.

Why is Sisi leaving?

Sisi became president in 2014, after the overthrow of Mohamed Morsi’s short-lived Muslim Brotherhood government. He is currently serving his third term, after winning elections seen as predetermined in 2018 and 2023. A constitutional referendum in 2019, also seen as predetermined, increased the president’s term from four to six years, extending Sisi’s current term to 2030.

Sisi, who is 71, did not give an exact reason for why he would step down in his speech at the military academy. He said that there would be no further amendments to Egypt’s constitution to prolong his rule and declared it ‘a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed,’ suggesting a transition of power is inevitable.  

Economic troubles

Two factors likely lie behind this surprise decision. 

First, the debt-financed economic model pursued under Sisi is unsustainable. This system has sustained military dominance and stalled urgent economic reform. The government’s vast borrowing to fund mega projects has created a structural economic crisis. 

In this year’s budget, debt servicing accounts for 63.9 per cent of planned expenditure, a significant increase from 43 per cent in 2014. Interest payments alone, as a share of GDP, exceed the combined allocations for education, healthcare, wages and subsidies combined. Egypt’s external debt rose from $46.1 billion in 2014 (16.4 per cent of GDP) to $164.8 billion (38.9 per cent of GDP) by the end of Q1 2026. 

The Egyptian pound exchange rate has plummeted from 7.14 per dollar in mid-2014 to about 53.8 per dollar in October 2026. Urban inflation has risen from 8.3 per cent in May 2014 to 13.9 per cent in September 2026 and is expected to rise further. 

This increased pressure on ordinary Egyptians has made the last decade one of plummeting living standards. Official data shows the national poverty rate has reached 35.7 per cent in 2023.

Public anger over rising living costs, combined with structural imbalances and rising debt, have made Sisi’s economic policies untenable – even among his allies.

The long-lasting economic crisis is an existential threat to the regime’s stability. Sisi himself may have calculated that Egypt urgently needs a new social contract to avoid economic-driven social unrest that could push him out or plunge the country into perpetual chaos. 

He will likely want to avoid the fate of President Hosni Mubarak, who was forced to leave office amid the January 25 Revolution in 2011. It is also likely that there will be an arrangement to protect Sisi and his family members from potential future prosecutions as a condition of him stepping down. 

Protecting the state 

The second factor relates to Sisi’s vision for his presidency and the state. This is fundamentally shaped by the 2011 uprising, which he has described as ‘the death certificate of the Egyptian state.’ 

Since he was sworn in in 2014, Sisi has repeatedly warned that another popular uprising would threaten the state’s existence. He has portrayed national prosperity as depending on excluding from Egypt’s politics what he frequently calls ‘ahl elshar’ (people of evil), often understood as referring to Islamists. He has also warned of threats to ‘national memory’ on social media. 

Sisi has portrayed it as his – and the military’s – national duty to spare Egypt the chaos engulfing other Arab Spring countries by removing the Muslim Brotherhood from power amid a popular uprising. He has indicated that he considers it his duty to reshape Egypt’s politics to guarantee long-term stability as he sees it.   

In his speech at the military academy, Sisi revealed that he had insisted on incorporating Article 200 into the 2019 constitutional amendments. This article effectively designates the military as the guardian of Egypt’s national, secular identity and the regime. 

Given this, Sisi may therefore feel that departing in 2030 is in line with his aims. The military-trained officials he has designated as his successors would serve as the practical implementers of this vision.

Military-shaped succession

Alongside his plans to step down, Sisi also announced that the armed forces will fund a 30-month military academy course to train potential future leaders. Egyptians will then be able to ‘elect and choose’ from among the graduates.

The course will train select candidates, who must have a PhD and be 40-50 years old, for positions including minister, member of parliament, governor, and potentially even president. Those who have served in government for at least six years will be exempted. 

Sisi’s choice of the military academy is not surprising, since it has long been tasked with promoting a military-centric nationalism and overseeing appointments and promotions in state institutions. This has sometimes sparked resistance, for example from judges in January. 

In effect, the system will replace the electoral process with competence criteria, narrowing the pool of trusted candidates and excluding anyone who is ‘tendentious, a traitor, or a criminal’ from becoming president. 

Future implications

Although this process finally paves the way for civilians to become president, the military will likely retain decisive influence over leadership selection and the state’s strategic direction. The military’s constitutional mandate means its commanders’ views and preferences would continue to shape key state decisions.

Related work

Should Egypt join the Mecca Pact?

In this setup, Sisi will likely retain entrenched loyalties and broader political influence. The changes could establish an informal military guardianship model that sits above the president and government beyond 2030. This might resemble Turkey in the 1990s.

The new government training system might also invite challenges. It seems designed to side-line dissidents, the Muslim Brotherhood and rival generals. But by effectively excluding individuals without a postgraduate degree or those who fail to secure academy approval, it might be deemed unconstitutional and face legal challenges. It could also spark fierce competition among key security branches.

Will Sisi reconsider?

Sisi’s decision to step down might face resistance from key institutions and influential figures in his patronage system, who may try to convince him to reconsider to protect their interests. 

These attempts may intensify if Egypt’s military becomes involved in escalating regional conflicts. Sisi recently sought authorization from parliament to deploy troops to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. 

If living conditions worsen and social unrest breaks out, Sisi may conclude that staying in power best guarantees stability for Egypt. 

Potential for civilian rule?

Despite its risks, Sisi’s decision may facilitate a transition towards a less authoritarian government in the long term. It took Egyptians 15 years after the 2011 uprising to hear an Egyptian president pledge an ordinary, peaceful transition of power. 

By declaring he will step down, Sisi could end up kickstarting a tradition in which no single ruler stays in power until death. Civilians might finally be seen as capable rulers. 

This will not happen overnight, of course. It would depend on Sisi keeping his word and social stability holding until 2030. But if this is the case, the military guardianship Sisi is establishing may, in the long term, be seen as a transitional period toward a more stable, more open and freer society.

title: Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine?
author: jon.wallace
description:
Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine? Expert comment jon.wallace 22 October 2026

Not immediately. But a Democratic victory could set the terms for a new approach by the next president.

Whatever the results, November’s midterm elections will not immediately transform US policy toward Israel and Palestine. In any outcome, the separation of powers means that President Donald Trump will still control American foreign policy. Even a Democrat-controlled Congress could not compel his administration to pursue a fundamentally different approach. 

But the midterms may accelerate a transformation that is already underway in the Democratic Party and among the US electorate, where the political centre of gravity on Israel and Palestine is shifting rapidly. 

If Democrats win a majority in either or both houses, they will gain new congressional tools to act on Israel–Palestine issues. Most importantly, the legislation they put forward would establish the policy baseline from which a future Democratic administration would govern.

The shift

Among dozens of others, Democrats like Abdul El-Sayed, running for the US Senate in Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres, running in the general against another Democrat in California, have drawn considerable attention for their criticism of Israeli government actions – and US support for them. The race in Michigan, which could be decisive for Democratic hopes to retake the senate, looks tight.

But even if progressive candidates don’t do as well as expected in these elections, a shift is underway. Developments in Washington over just the past month illustrate how much has already changed.

On 29 September, 46 of 47 Senate Democrats voted for a resolution led by Senators Chris Van Hollen, Tim Kaine and Bernie Sanders. This would ‘require the Department of State to provide information and assessments related to investigations of the killing of United States citizens by violent Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces in the West Bank’. The resolution did not pass the Republican majority. But the vote was remarkable for its unanimity. Such Democratic unity on a resolution critical of Israel would have been almost unimaginable only a few years ago.

The vote follows a distinct trajectory in Democratic politics. When Senator Bernie Sanders forced the Senate to vote on blocking weapon sales to Israel in November 2024, only 18 Democrat senators supported him. This April, 40 of 47 Senate Democrats voted against a sale of bulldozers to Israel. And 36 opposed the sale of 1,000-pound bombs. Now, with the September resolution, virtually the entire Senate Democratic caucus has voted to demand accountability from Israel.

Become a corporate member

Give your organization access to trusted geopolitical analysis, policy insight and expert networks to help leaders anticipate risk, navigate uncertainty and make informed decisions.

Then came the House of Representatives. On 1 October, Rep. Joaquin Castro and other members introduced the Stop the Settlements Act. This builds on the Biden administration’s 2024 sanctions on violent Israeli extremists in the West Bank, which saw a major power set up a process to sanction those undermining peace and threatening violence in the West Bank. 

It also builds on the subsequent 2026 sanctions by European countries and Canada against products originating in Israeli settlements. The Act would impose sanctions on individuals and entities responsible for building or expanding Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank or Gaza and prohibit settlement goods from entering the US market. 

These developments point toward an emerging Democratic Party position: one that more actively defends the rights of the Palestinian people and is more willing to seek to compel Israel and the White House to move in that direction. Notably, Barack Obama’s planned 24 October event with El-Sayed on the campaign trail shows a greater willingness by the party’s elite to accommodate criticism of Israeli policies.

That shift matters. Israel and Palestine remain secondary issues for most US voters, compared to the economy, healthcare, education and other domestic concerns. But firm convictions on Israel–Palestine have become important attributes for some candidates in Democratic party politics. And the midterms will, in some ways, be a referendum on how criticism of Israeli policies affects voter intentions – with candidates like El-Sayed calling Israeli actions in Gaza a genocide, a claim the Netanyahu government strenuously denies. 

But one thing looks certain: US views on the Israeli government have become less favourable across age groups and political parties. Even among American Jews, 61 per cent believe Israel is guilty of war crimes and 39 per cent call it genocide, according to a 2025 Washington Post poll. The tide may already have decisively shifted, regardless of whether or not candidates like El-Sayed win their races. 

A Democratic Congress

Democratic takeover of the House and the Senate would make the shift more consequential immediately. Much of Congress’s influence over foreign policy occurs not through dramatic floor votes, but through the accumulation of hearings, letters, reporting requirements, funding restrictions and private pressure on administrations. 

Democratic-controlled committees could hold hearings on settlement expansion in the West Bank and settler violence, scrutinize US arms sales to Israel, demand administration briefings, investigate the treatment of American citizens, mark-up legislation and use appropriations and oversight to press the executive branch. 

House and Senate Democrats should begin laying the groundwork to create an affirmative American Palestine policy. That is, a policy not only defined by a move to restrict Israeli settlement-building and the sale of weapons to Israel, but one that advocates for Palestinian self-determination and an architecture for advancing it. 

Over the decades, Congress has constructed a dense web of laws that restrict American relations with the PLO and the Palestinian Authority. A Democratic Congress could therefore begin to map those restrictions and decide how to address them. Which can be addressed administratively? Which need Congressional amendment or repeal? What policy changes will the US seek from the Palestinian leadership? 

This will not be straightforward: Democrats are still debating these policies, and unanimity will not always be possible: there remains a diversity of views and priorities within the party. 

Congress also needs far greater exposure to Palestinian political, economic and civil-society leaders. While many US politicians routinely engage with every dimension of Israeli politics, few have sustained relationships with Palestinians who can explain Palestinian institutions, aspirations and internal debates.

Two time horizons

Were candidates like El-Sayed to lose their races, and were midterms results to be disappointing for the Democrats, it is possible that some in the party might hesitate about the trajectory on Israel and Palestine policy.

But, assuming Democrats gain control of Congress, they could use 2027 and 2028 to constrain, oversee and prepare. A Democratic Congress could press Israel for accountability for violence against Palestinians and Americans, challenge settlement expansion, scrutinize US military assistance, support viable elements of Gaza reconstruction, strengthen Palestinian institutions and begin removing legal obstacles to normal US-Palestinian relations.

These preparations will be significant if a Democrat returns to the White House in 2029. A new administration will be best able to move forward a markedly different policy if significant progress is made in the previous two years.

In this respect, though the midterms will not be the moment US policy toward Israel and Palestine changes, they can set the context for any Democrat running in the presidential primaries – which essentially begin as soon as the new Congress is seated. 

Those who have been advocating for Palestinian rights for decades now see that not only their elected representatives, but the next US president may align with them as well. 

That will not fix anything today for the relatives of the more than 70,000 Palestinians killed in Gaza, the millions that continue to suffer in the occupied territories, or Israelis dealing with the aftermath of the Hamas cross-border attacks of 7 October 2023. But it does provide a modicum of hope that there is a pathway to freedom and liberty for all. What we’ll learn from the US midterms is how quickly that change is likely to come.

title: Imbalances are a feature of the global financial system, not a bug
author: jon.wallace
description:
Imbalances are a feature of the global financial system, not a bug  Expert comment jon.wallace 17 September 2026

The current focus on ‘global imbalances’ is too easily used by policymakers as a smokescreen for their own domestic failings.

Global imbalances are back on the international finance agenda this year, prompting a flagship G7 report and creating discord at the G20 finance minsters’ summit. 

Seemingly this focus on global imbalances is justified. China’s trade in goods surplus now alarms Europe’s leaders as much as it worries America’s. The US’s net liability to the world – the degree to which its overseas borrowing exceeds its overseas investments – reached an astonishing 70 per cent of US GDP in 2025. The last time global imbalances were this prominent was just ahead of 2008’s Global Financial Crisis.

What a shame, then, that this focus is so misguided. Imbalances are a feature of the global financial system, not a bug. They arise from saving and investment decisions, allowing diversification and dispersing risk in the process. In truth, ‘global imbalances’ are not primarily a global phenomenon. They are simply the product of all the world’s domestic imbalances added up. 

And because foreign investment is more mobile than domestic investment, it is more likely to punish bad domestic policymaking by moving elsewhere. The result is to impose discipline – constraints – on political choices.

There is a generous interpretation of the motives for the current focus on global imbalances. It is possible that simultaneous domestic reforms across the global economy would make fixing economic issues at home easier for everyone.

But the tone and outcomes at the G20 minsters’ summit invite a less generous conclusion; that some governments are attempting to dress up their domestic policy failings as the result of foreign actions.

A problem shared

For all the hand-wringing that global imbalances generate, you could be forgiven for forgetting that they reflect the global economy operating as it should. 

International risk-sharing is a primary benefit of economic openness. Take the US as an illustration. Its net liability of 70 per cent of GDP certainly looks eye-popping and far outstrips the biggest surpluses elsewhere. But look closer at what’s going on. 

First, the US issues the world’s reserve asset, US Treasuries. These are the global saving instrument of choice because they are safe, underpinned by a huge economy and the rule of law, and highly liquid – making them easy to buy and sell. 

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

Second, the US economy has outperformed the rest of the world in recent years, driven by its tech boom. Put simply, investment opportunities in the US outstrip US saving.

Far from being a nefarious ‘transfer of wealth’ out of the US, this is exactly how the global financial system is supposed to work. The US economy has generated huge investment opportunities. 

The world has open capital accounts to diversify risk: non-Americans can diversify away from risky or sluggish domestic assets to high-performing American ones. Americans don’t have to bear all the risk, because the rest of the world is putting money in too. This is textbook, win-win international risk-sharing.

And it illustrates a deeper point. Global imbalances don’t arise because of global phenomena. Rather, they arise because of domestic choices about saving and investment. Global imbalances are just the sum of these domestic imbalances.

No free lunches

Sharing risk and eliminating risk are not the same thing. Openness brings its own challenges, most obviously that overseas investors are ‘flightier’ – that is, more likely to swiftly withdraw investment – than domestic investors. They don’t have a ‘home bias’, are not engaged in domestic political choices, and may worry that, as foreign nationals, legal protections for their investments are less robust.

Do these flighty investors and global imbalances presage a rerun of the Global Financial Crisis? No. That crisis was caused by lax financial standards in Europe and the US, not the fabled ‘Global Savings Glut’. 

Even today’s huge US net liability looks robust. US liabilities are in dollars. Its assets are in foreign currency. So, if investors rebalance away from the US, the dollar depreciates. That raises the (dollar) value of US external assets, stabilizing the overall external position. That’s risk-sharing in action.

Instead, putting together foreign investors and domestic imbalances should have a disciplining effect. In response to bad policymaking, foreign investors can start to take their money elsewhere, lessening the likelihood of policymakers making bad domestic choices. 

Fundamentally, ‘global imbalances’ are most interesting for what they tell us about domestic decision-making. And today’s imbalances are flagging genuinely questionable choices by national governments.

The US government, for instance, spends too much borrowed money. At nearly 125 per cent of GDP, the US government’s gross debt is greater than the US’s entire external liabilities (or what it collectively owes the world). US Treasury yields have been rising, prompting exotic policy responses and putting pressure on the unsustainable US fiscal position.

Europeans, meanwhile, aren’t creating investment opportunities. Their savings are therefore flowing to where returns are more attractive – especially US AI investment. That lack of investment has allowed competitiveness to erode, leaving Europe falling further behind the US and vulnerable to Chinese competition.

At the same time, China spends too little. It funnels its savings into excessive investment, inflating asset bubbles and depressing consumption. After its housing bubble collapsed, exports surged but demand – including for imports – has remained feeble, alienating other major economies.

In each case the appropriate domestic policy prescription is obvious – but the political will is lacking.

Stones and glasshouses

The great hope, eloquently made by Hélène Rey, is that, by linking these individual challenges, a broad common interest might emerge and lead to positive simultaneous action, either through persuasion or peer pressure. Any fiscal consolidation enacted by the US, for instance, could be offset by rising investment in Europe and consumption in China. That would make the economics of adjustment easier. And, with everyone acting together, it could make the politics of adjustment easier too.

Related work

Global trade imbalances have changed since the 2008 financial crisis. Now they reflect new risks

Unfortunately, a less positive motive for the recent focus on imbalances is also possible. To the untrained ear ‘global’ imbalances sound like a global problem. And blaming overseas developments for domestic problems is a seductive narrative in political discourse. Indeed, it can already clearly be observed through easily falsified claims that imports steal jobs, or that a reserve currency issuer must run deficits. And it can be seen in poorly targeted policies like tariffs, which do nothing to address the underlying issues.

And recent international meetings confirm that global policymakers are failing to take ambitious, simultaneous action. For instance, rather than leading by example, the G7 failed to agree either fiscal consolidation in the US or accelerated structural reform in Europe. Instead, they punted the issue to August’s G20 finance ministers’ summit, which then failed to agree on a communiqué. The language that emerged in the ‘chair’s statement’ was noticeably tougher on surplus countries than on deficit countries. And the US was not shy about blaming China for the failure to reach agreement.

Global imbalances are not in themselves an imminent risk. Rather, they are a credible early warning signal of domestic problems. By placing so much emphasis on the global dimension and failing to follow through with credible action, policymakers risk undermining the case for difficult domestic reform, rather than advancing it. As the unfashionable Washington Consensus used to have it, the key to prosperity is putting your own house in order, not casting stones at your neighbours.

title: China is weathering the Hormuz energy crisis. But copying its model comes with risks
author: thilton.drupal
description:
China is weathering the Hormuz energy crisis. But copying its model comes with risks Expert comment thilton.drupal 17 September 2026

China absorbed the shock by drawing on stockpiles and a decade of electrification. Europe needs electrification for security, but it needs to decide which parts of the system it is willing to buy from Beijing.

Resources are no longer ‘king’ when it comes to energy, wrote Zhao Hongtu and Chen Wenlin in the 1 September 2026 edition of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship theoretical journal. Mineral-rich economies may have some leverage, but the countries that control ‘transition-related technology, finance and rules’ will gain more influence as the world sees the rise of the ‘electrostate’, with ‘China, India and Brazil becoming the main force of new energy development.’

As a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, argue Zhao and Chen, energy security has become a priority in national policymaking: ‘clean energy is seen as an important route to security’ and ‘economies that actively embrace the energy transition may occupy more important positions in the future global energy landscape.’

It is unsurprising that a CCP journal would commend China’s efforts in building renewable energy and managing the fallout of the Iran war. But the numbers support their conclusions. The oil importer most exposed to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz – China imports 70 per cent of its oil, around half of it from the Gulf – has also been the least disrupted. 

Weathering the storm

China’s strength in weathering the Hormuz crisis so far stands in contrast to much of the world. 

The crisis pushed the 32 members of the International Energy Agency (spanning the oil importers of the rich world) to carry out their largest-ever emergency stock release, aimed at stopping oil prices from spiralling further. They released more than 400 million barrels in total, including 172 million from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, to replace some of the 20 million barrels per day (b/d) that had been passing through Hormuz. 

China needed no such collective effort. Beijing entered the crisis with an estimated 1.4 billion barrels in storage: around 360 million in government reserves and the rest in commercial tanks, totalling at least three months of imports. 

In response to Hormuz, China diversified its imports: roughly one-third of the barrels it lost from the Gulf were replaced from elsewhere, such as Brazil, according to the Asia Group. 

The rest of these lost imports went unreplaced: China’s crude imports fell by a third, from 12 million b/d on the eve of the war to less than 8 million b/d in May and June. 

About 60 per cent of the shortfall from unreplaced imports was met from storage. The rest was not met; instead, there was a real fall in the amount of oil China burned. Refineries cut their crude runs and Beijing ordered the big state refiners to halt fuel exports so that what they did produce stayed at home. 

Electrification and security

China was able to survive this fall in oil consumption due to the electrification of its economy. An electrified economy can use less oil without using less transport. Electric vehicles accounted for more than 60 per cent of domestic monthly vehicle sales in the first half of 2026. Drivers of conventional automobiles reportedly switched to electric ride-hailing.

Chinese clean technology has been manufactured and deployed at scales that have driven the cost of equipment down substantially. China leads the world in renewable power installation. In the first half of 2026, China added more wind capacity than in any full calendar year before 2025.

Want to hear more on the path to a secure energy transition?

Join us at our climate and energy summit, where policymakers and industry leaders tackle the toughest questions on climate and energy security.

This resilience is not a happy coincidence or an unintended benefit of climate policy. The Hormuz crisis validated long-term strategic concerns in China. Back in 2003, CCP General Secretary Hu Jintao coined the term ‘Malacca Dilemma,’ referring to the energy chokepoint in the Strait of Malacca. Since then, energy security has underpinned Beijing’s low-carbon industrial strategy.

China’s 15th Five Year Plan (2026-2030), adopted in March, formalized this green energy statecraft. As analyst Lu Ruquan summarizes, the plan’s energy framework aims to provide China with the energy security needed to weather crises by ‘increasing oil and gas reserves and production, stabilizing annual crude oil output at 200 million tonnes, replacing petroleum consumption, and securing the supply of critical mineral resources for new energy.’

The plan’s approach is convincing. Within this, electrification helps governments to hedge against volatile pricing, a weaponized dollar, and an increasingly uncertain geopolitical environment. 

China’s dominance of renewables

This is particularly clear for Asian economies increasingly embracing renewables. Indonesia’s president, for example, has pushed for an all-electric transport transition to reduce import reliance.  

Southeast Asian nations have spent over $20 billion on Chinese-made clean-tech products so far in 2026, according to a recent Reuters analysis citing the think-tank Ember. China makes much of the hardware used in renewable projects, such as panels, inverters, turbines or battery storage. 

In 2024, China produced more than 90 per cent of the polysilicon, wafers and cells, and 86 per cent of the modules needed for solar energy globally. The figures are similar in other industries like batteries, where graphite and anode active materials, for example, are largely concentrated in Chinese supply chains. 

China is also financing green energy at record levels across the Global South, totalling approximately $20.1 billion in the first half of 2026, more than all of 2025. 

Different dependencies

But for middle powers, this security hedge is double edged. While the transition away from oil and gas can help protect against energy shocks, the concentration of clean technology in China could leave states dependent on Beijing. 

The World Today

Related work

What the West fails to grasp about China’s strategy to lead the world

The green transition is reliant on critical minerals and rare earths. For many of these materials, China controls much of the global refining and mining, giving Beijing an effective tool of statecraft. For example, Beijing halted exports of rare earths to Japan in January amid rising tensions between the two countries related to Taiwan.

Similarly, China could leverage its dominance in the production of solar panels, EVs and other green technologies. 

This risk is different to that of relying on fossil fuels. Disruptions to oil and gas have an immediate impact that can be felt in higher prices. No navy can blockade the sun or wind. 

But depending on China’s low-carbon technologies and critical inputs may impact countries’ ability to implement the green transition more broadly, rather than hitting short-term supply. 

Europe needs to think strategically 

This is increasingly recognized in Europe. ‘We still have too many dangerous dependencies,’ said European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in her State of the Union on Wednesday. ‘We are more than 80 per cent dependent on China for many critical raw materials. 90 per cent for some rare earths… We need to urgently procure and build up our reserves.’ 

This autumn, EU officials will face this reality as they attempt to settle the bloc’s trade posture towards China and the final shape of the Industrial Accelerator Act rules, aimed at boosting European manufacturing. The UK faces a similarly complex set of questions around competition, security and decarbonization.  

Europe should not slow its transition. Instead, China’s example highlights Europe’s need to embrace its own green energy statecraft. Europe needs to accelerate diversification and reduce exposure to chokepoints – whether in fossil fuels or other energy-related supply chains. That does not mean rebuilding the whole supply chain. It means being selective, as Europe has demonstrated by tightening the rules around critical components like inverters. 

Done right, this should not only reduce Europe’s vulnerability to Chinese supply weaponization, but also hedge against US policy volatility and potential political interference. European officials and experts have warned, for example, that the Trump administration could potentially seek to use Europe’s dependency on US gas as leverage to dictate terms over issues like Greenland or tariffs. 

Perhaps it’s time for Europe to think about its own sources of leverage. It may yet need to deploy them as geoeconomic deterrence. Both the US and China have shown they will use supply as a weapon; a Europe that cannot answer in kind will have its energy choices made for it.

title: Foreign rivalries risk turning Somalia’s political crisis into a protracted war
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Foreign rivalries risk turning Somalia’s political crisis into a protracted war Expert comment thilton.drupal 15 October 2026

Somalia’s domestic instability is being compounded by sharpened regional rivalries, paving the way for a more entrenched conflict as seen elsewhere in the Horn of Africa.

Somalia has been embroiled in a political crisis since May 2026, when the term of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was originally due to expire. Parliament passed constitutional amendments in March that extended presidential terms to five years, keeping President Hassan Sheikh in office until May 2027. 

This was disputed by Somalia’s opposition alliance, a coalition of political figures including the leadership of the federal member states of Puntland in the north and Jubaland in the south, as well as the former president of South West State, Abdiaziz Laftagareen. This week, the opposition also rejected the electoral commission’s unilateral announcement that parliamentary and presidential polls would take place in April and May 2027.

The political crisis has sparked fierce clashes in Mogadishu and the city of Baidoa in South West State. The recent fighting around Baidoa, between government forces and opposition-allied fighters loyal to Laftagreen, reportedly involved thousands of fighters and the use of drones and fighter jets. 

The federal government, along with its allied federal member state administrations – South West, Hirshabelle, and Galmudug – controls most major cities in southern and central Somalia, while Jubaland, in the far south, is at odds with Mogadishu. Al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda-affiliated organization, controls much of the surrounding countryside. Meanwhile, the administrations of Puntland and the self-declared Republic of Somaliland govern much of the north, with the newly created and federal government-aligned North East State squeezed in-between. 

High stakes amid regional tensions

This is not Somalia’s first experience of constitutional disputes leading to armed clashes, with similar conflict occurring in 2021. But the stakes are higher this time, as the balance of power within the federal system is at stake. The opposition accuses the current federal government under President Hassan Sheikh of seeking to consolidate power in Mogadishu at the expense of the states.

Related work

War has returned to Tigray. This time it may not stay in Ethiopia

The conflict in Somalia is also taking place in a region that has increasingly become the focus of escalating rivalries between foreign powers in a complex web of alliances. Two broad, fluid blocs have taken shape: Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkey are seen as broadly aligned with Sudan’s Armed Forces and Eritrea in the region, while the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Israel are seen as broadly aligned with Ethiopia. 

In Somalia’s current political crisis, Turkey and the UAE are the two most important external actors. Turkey is seen as backing the federal government, while the UAE has relations with the opposition state administrations. 

These dynamics are helping to both incentivize new alliances and deepen divisions. Given the existing domestic volatility, there is a serious compound risk of newly entrenched conflict. 

Turkey and the UAE

Turkey has been engaged in Somalia for over a decade, primarily but not exclusively through the federal government in Mogadishu. Its initial involvement concentrated on humanitarian and development initiatives. It has also run a military training camp for the Somali armed forces since 2017.

Turkey has drawn closer to the Hassan Sheikh administration since 2024 after signing several strategic agreements with Mogadishu. This prompted some opposition figures to question Turkey’s neutrality in the context of the current conflict over the presidential term extension. Turkey has rejected accusations of political interference and says its position is consistent with its support for Somalia’s federal government institutions. 

However, more recently, Turkish fighter jets were reportedly involved in the fighting near Baidoa. This has not been confirmed by Ankara, but would constitute a notable direct intervention against armed political opposition. 

The UAE established multi-layered ties with the current federal government and some of the country’s federal member states. However, in January 2026, Somalia’s federal government annulled all its defence and security cooperation agreements with the UAE, accusing it of undermining Somalia’s national sovereignty. 

This move coincided with the Saudi-Emirati rift in Yemen. Days before annulling the agreements, Somalia launched an investigation after the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen accused Abu Dhabi of facilitating the evacuation of a Yemeni separatist leader to the UAE via Berbera and Mogadishu. Somalia then signed defence agreements with Saudi Arabia and Qatar, with diplomatic support from Turkey and Egypt.

The UAE has maintained direct relations with Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland, with Emirati firms maintaining significant interests in port operations. All of these regional administrations had rejected the cancellation of the agreements by Mogadishu. 

Retaining influence with the leadership in each territory is therefore critical to the UAE’s wider strategy in the Horn of Africa. But its relations with the federal states opposed to Mogadishu are contributing to further inflaming tensions.  

Domestic drivers 

Local actors are also increasingly looking outwards for foreign backing to shore up their domestic interests and legitimacy. To attract support, both the federal government and the opposition are making efforts to show that their domestic influence aligns with the interests of external actors. 

This appeal to foreign players is driven by multiple factors. Key among them is the profound political division among Somali political actors, and the persistent failure to genuinely address these divisions. To counterbalance their local political rivals, competing domestic elites are therefore seeking to offer strategic incentives to external powers such as port investments, economic partnerships, transport corridors and military bases.

The federal government’s controversial constitutional and electoral reforms have solidified these divisions. Some federal member states and Somaliland feel threatened by Mogadishu’s consolidation of power, backed by Turkey’s reported military support and investments. 

Shifting regional geopolitical dynamics are also increasing the leverage available to domestic actors in Somalia. The Houthis’ advance in Yemen has once again exposed the importance of the Bab al-Mandab Strait connecting the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea, reinforcing Somalia’s strategic location. The Houthis reportedly have growing relations with al-Shabaab in Somalia.  

The risks of deepening war

Somalia has been embroiled in armed conflicts for over three decades. No single entity – whether a clan, a specific administration or a regional government – has been able to dominate the rest and rule the entire country. 

However, the escalation of current armed clashes between political opponents, and the involvement of more sophisticated weaponry, points to a new chapter. Local actors are increasingly seeking external support and new alliances as a counterbalance to rising threats. 

For example, a minister from Laftagareen’s former South West State administration recently stated that their forces used drones in the latest Baidoa conflict and said they would accept drones from any external power. In the north, Puntland and Somaliland formed an alliance in response to the federal government establishing North East State in 2025. These dynamics risk a widening conflict fuelled by the support of foreign powers. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Furthermore, these armed conflicts provide an opportunity for terrorist organizations active in Somalia, such as al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia. During political crises, security operations against these groups often decline considerably, allowing them to recover and regroup. The deepening armed conflicts between the federal government and opposition groups offers these organizations an opportunity to expand their influence within a multi-layered conflict.   

Given these broader stakes, it is in the interests of all external parties who have relations with the federal government and member states to pursue options for de-escalation between Somali political actors. Considering their intersection with wider regional dynamics in the Horn of Africa and Red Sea, it is also vital that de-escalation efforts are triangulated through regional institutions such as the African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). 

In the short term, there is a need to facilitate dialogue that can pave the way for an inclusive political agreement on constitutional amendments, electoral issues and interim governance arrangements, with a realistic timetable until elections can be held. Without such an agreement, the risk of a wider protracted conflict will continue to rise.
