title: Sánchez’s gamble: This ‘all-in’ election will have international impact
author: jon.wallace
description:
Sánchez’s gamble: This ‘all-in’ election will have international impact Expert comment jon.wallace 5 October 2026

Announcing the election, Sánchez set himself in opposition to President Trump and Javier Milei as well as Spain’s populist right. Much will depend on the prime minister’s ability to rally a fragmented left.

The decision by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election is a risky move, but he will have felt he had little choice. His decision fires the starting gun on a year of vital and polarized elections across Europe.

The announcement is not entirely unexpected. Spain was required to hold an election by August 2027 anyway. And Sánchez’s multiparty coalition has looked fragile since it formed in July 2023: it has not passed a full budget since. 

In January, the government approved a decree that regularized the status of 500,000 undocumented migrants and asylum seekers – a move unusual among EU countries generally committed to tightening migration restrictions. In July, the Spanish enclave of Ceuta was overwhelmed by a surge of tens of thousands of migrants, leading to criticism of government policy from within Spain and abroad, including US President Donald Trump. 

This month, a new issue has arisen, as protests grow over housing affordability. The protests prompted the government to introduce emergency legislation, only to see the bill rejected by Spain’s Parliament late last week. This gave Sánchez his opening to call a general election, arguing that ‘to do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people’. 

What are Sánchez’s chances?

Sánchez is a proven survivor and faced similar difficulties in 2023. But calling an election now is a gamble. The summer’s crises have given his political opponents plenty to work with, and trouble assails the prime minister and his party, the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), from every side. 

The opposition on the right will use the January decree and images of the Ceuta crisis to rally their vote and criticize the government’s competence. The left will point out the housing crisis has deteriorated under Sánchez. Then there are the corruption scandals that plague the prime minister. Some of his closest political allies are embroiled in the Koldo case – an investigation into corruption in health procurement contracts during the COVID-19 pandemic. In a separate case, the prime minister’s own wife has been charged with embezzlement and corruption.

To survive, Sánchez will use the same playbook that worked for him in 2023, where he characterized the contest as a choice between ‘Sanchismo’ (his brand of social democrat politics) or a ‘backward-looking’ far right. 

Related work

The Ceuta border crisis heaps pressure on Spain’s Sánchez government – and European unity

His hope will be that opposition to the PP right wing opposition party – and far right Vox party in particular – will mobilize left wing voters in a highly polarized contest. Vox leader Santiago Abascal regularly speaks of a ‘migrant invasion’ and used Sanchez’s January decree to call for ‘Repatriations, deportations and remigration’. 

Notably, Sánchez’s speech on the steps of La Moncloa (the Spanish prime minister’s residence) put international talking points at the centre of his pitch, contrasting his positions with the those of the right, and particularly US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei:

‘We have strived to build a better world for our fellow citizens and for the rest of humanity,’ he said, ‘supporting Ukraine, the European Union, and the United Nations in their darkest moments. Denouncing genocidal regimes when others remained silent.

‘Fighting tyrants, techno-oligarchs, and speculators who want to destroy the future of our sons and daughters to enlarge their pockets. Doubling our aid to international cooperation while others boasted of cutting it with their chainsaw or on that military altar of 5 per cent of GDP.’

Spain’s voting system

50 days of intense campaigning and negotiation between parties will now follow. These negotiations matter because of Spain’s electoral system. 

Spain uses the D’Hondt method in provincial constituencies, which punishes parties polling in low single figures. Small parties can survive by running together on a joint list, but past attempts have had mixed results. 

Sumar is the largest of these groupings. Despite having no leader, it has launched ‘Frente Amplio’ (the Broad Front) to try to pull support together. Much will depend on the firebrand MP Gabriel Rufián. He is seen as a potential unifier of the fragmented parties to the left of PSOE. But he is not a Sumar figure, and internal politics and personalities have a habit of wrecking electoral pacts in Spain. Podemos, PSOE’s coalition partner, joined Sumar’s list in 2023 but broke away within months.

For Sánchez, what happens to his left matters more than ever. His pitch therefore needs to be binary. Expect him to use Trump, Milei and Flávio Bolsonaro (ahead in Brazil’s presidential race after the first round) as bogeymen to focus minds even before the ballots are printed.

On the right, the Partido Popular (PP) will likely approach a ‘Ming Vase strategy’ of trying to just get through the next 50 days without any major mishaps. It is not clear that this can work. Questions about what a coalition with Vox would look like will follow their leader Alberto Feijóo. His inability to respond adequately to such questions in 2023 likely cost him victory. 

Spain’s vote will now be the first in a series of crucial European elections. France chooses a new president in spring 2027. Italy, Poland, Finland and Greece are due to vote before the year is out. Many of these contests will look like Spain’s, with some seeing fragile coalitions on the left facing a confident and surging right. 

The results will matter well beyond domestic politics. For instance, as the US continues to demand the continent do more for its own defence, disruptive elections will make it harder to make progress on a more coherent joint European approach to security. This campaign will be closely followed across the continent – and from across the Atlantic – as politicians seek to perfect their pitch in ever more polarized times.

title: Nepal’s floods put the global loss and damage system to the test
author: jon.wallace
description:
Nepal’s floods put the global loss and damage system to the test Expert comment jon.wallace 5 October 2026

Nepal’s recovery from August’s catastrophic glacial flood will test the efficiency of the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. It will also resurface questions about the responsibilities of the greatest carbon emitters.

On 26 August 2026, a glacial disaster high in the Himalayas sent a wall of meltwater and debris tearing through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Rasuwa region at speeds of nearly 188 km per hour. The flood has claimed over 1400 lives, with thousands still missing.  

Nepal is experiencing the consequences of a warming cryosphere, with accelerated glacier melt that could undermine the long-term security of a water source on which millions of people depend.  

The country only contributes around 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet its people are on the front lines of climate change impacts, as glacial retreat reshapes the Himalayan landscape. Early estimates of the cost of reconstruction are $4 to 5 billion, around a tenth of Nepal’s GDP. 

Nepal’s government has appealed to the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) for help. But that can only provide a fraction of the funds required. As a result, Nepal has raised the responsibility of the world’s largest carbon emitters and will bring the issue to the forefront of November’s COP31 climate summit in Turkey.

In this respect, Nepal’s recovery will stress-test bigger questions: How far is it possible to establish whether climate change was a contributing factor to a disaster? Can international climate finance mechanisms deliver urgent help to countries facing imminent, irreparable losses? And what more should the world’s greatest emitters be doing to help countries like Nepal?

The Fund faces a credibility test

Since the FRLD was established at COP27 in 2022, demand for financial support has far exceeded available funding. As of March 2026, 27 countries pledged $822.06 million, of which only around half was received. The Fund made $342 million available in its first round, dwarfed by requests of close to $2.8 billion for losses and damages worldwide.

The Fund faces disbursement delays from unreliable capital flows and institutional bottlenecks, due to unfulfilled voluntary commitments and approval processes within the World Bank. Nepal’s access is also constrained by complex, multi-tiered federal approval processes and lengthy procurement procedures.

At present, there is no rapid-access pathway for countries to apply for FRLD funding outside scheduled application windows. Questions also remain about how the Fund will assess the role of climate change in causing particular disasters, and how such assessments might influence funding decisions.

Nepal has emerged as an early test of how the Fund will respond. Kathmandu has requested $20 million – a modest sum compared to the scale of economic damage. Yet the request is significant for what it reveals about the Fund’s ability to respond in practice: Can the Fund move resources quickly and predictably enough to provide support when it is most needed?

Scientific attribution 

Nepal’s catastrophe puts attribution front and centre: how can it be established whether climate change was a contributing factor to a disaster, rather than the sole cause? If it is found to be a contributing factor, when is that sufficient to establish harm? And is it possible to apportion responsibility for global warming to greenhouse gas emissions by certain countries?

Nepal is relying on a recent flood study in its claim to the Fund, attributing several cascading climate factors to the onset of this catastrophe. This should make Nepal’s case for loss and damage straightforward. The harm is tangible, the science exists, and the FRLD was built for this scenario. But a fund capped at $20 million per project is facing a disaster impact estimated in billions. That may push Nepal to look past the Fund’s limits to the countries whose emissions may have contributed to these harms. 

In July 2025, the International Court of Justice’s Advisory Opinion on Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change offered a real, if partial, legal scaffolding to claims that states suffering climate-related harm may seek address, a development relevant to Nepal’s application to the FRLD. On establishing harm, the Court accepted that climate science can be relied upon to link specific disasters to climate change. A ‘sufficiently direct and certain’ standard was set to accommodate the complexity of determining causality in climate events. 

Responding to losses and damages 

Speaking at the UN General Assembly last Friday, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah argued that the FRLD and other mechanisms remain ‘grossly inadequate’ for countries like his, which contributed little to warming of the Himalayan climate. This followed calls by his foreign minister for major emitters to work together to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal. 

By seeking support from major emitters across developed and developing countries, Nepal is challenging established understandings of climate responsibility and raising difficult questions about who should bear the costs of climate-related losses. 

Want to hear more on the path to a secure energy transition?

Join us at our climate and energy summit, where policymakers and industry leaders tackle the toughest questions on climate and energy security.

Though politically significant, translating that into an international financing obligation will be difficult. While China and India’s present-day emissions are substantial, India’s per capita emissions and both their historical contributions are low relative to other advanced economies. 

Both are considered developing countries under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and argue for differentiated responsibilities to developed countries like the United States under Article 2 (2) of the Paris Agreement. Meanwhile, the US withdrawal from UNFCCC creates financial, governance and diplomatic challenges ahead of COP31. 

However, both China and India have significant interests in Nepalese recovery. Both invest heavily in infrastructure development in the ecologically fragile region, while India relies on Nepal’s hydropower. And both countries’ proximity to Nepal creates shared priorities in Himalayan resilience. 

Furthermore, their responsibilities to address climate change can evolve as domestic capabilities and emission profiles grow, also helping to strengthen south-south cooperation. Addressing Nepal’s losses and damages therefore provides a strategic and humanitarian imperative, requiring a collective response to rebuild Nepal. 

COP31: The next test 

Questions of attribution and compensation are best left outside of negotiation rooms to appropriate legal forums. Instead, Nepal’s experience points to three priorities at this year’s COP31 summit. First, clearer standards are needed for attributing harm where multiple factors have contributed to a disaster. Second, more consistent approaches are required for establishing the value of economic and non-economic losses in cases like Nepal’s. Third, access to FRLD finance should be faster and more predictable. 

The political context will make progress difficult. COP31 comes amid geopolitical fragmentation, fiscal pressures and growing strain on multilateral cooperation. At the same time, some progress may be in sight. Loss and damage is formally on the agenda, including guidance to the FRLD, while the Fund prepares for its first funding decisions. Some scope for regional cooperation may remain, as illustrated by Prime Minister Shah’s proposal at the UN for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism between Nepal, India and China to share glacial-lake data and strengthen joint early-warning systems.  

Overall, Nepal’s application will provide a practical test of whether COP31 can move beyond broad commitments on loss and damage towards clearer rules for climate attribution, assessment and access to finance. The immediate opportunity may be incremental rather than transformational. Negotiators will need to establish processes that can be strengthened over time, while ensuring that disputes over responsibility do not prevent vulnerable countries receiving the support they need. However, more cases like Nepal’s will follow. And the need for a just solution to help countries recover from such disasters will only grow.

title: New energy and trade routes could bypass Hormuz and change the Middle East. But major challenges remain
author: thilton.drupal
description:
New energy and trade routes could bypass Hormuz and change the Middle East. But major challenges remain Expert comment thilton.drupal 25 September 2026

The Strait of Hormuz crisis is accelerating a wider reordering of the region, as Iraq, Syria and Lebanon plan new oil pipelines and transport corridors. But whether they can seize the opportunity to diversify will ultimately depend on wider reforms.

The war on Iran and the resulting disruption to the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the vulnerability of existing trade and energy routes and unsettled the old balance of power across the Middle East.

In this context, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon are seeking to capitalize on their position between Europe and the Gulf and improve their connectivity via oil and gas pipelines, roads, railways and digital corridors. Once central to an Iranian regional order, all three governments are now aiming to achieve greater sovereignty by diversifying their economic ties, a shift supported by the Trump administration. 

Yet they are attempting to do so while facing foreign occupations and military action, and while also confronting domestic endemic corruption and fragmented political systems that empower armed groups. 

Whether they can seize this opportunity to become more connected – and more sovereign – will therefore depend not only on the infrastructure they build, but on whether they can reform their states to govern it.

Changing energy routes

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused severe disruption to regional energy flows, including from Iraq. 

Pre-war, Iraq was exporting around 3.3 million b/d from its southern oilfields. By the second week of March, exports from southern Iraq had collapsed. Southern exports gradually recovered from mid-April, reaching 2.3 million b/d in August, aided by Iraq giving discounts for buyers and by Iran reportedly giving permission for Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait.

Syria and Lebanon have been less directly impacted by Hormuz, given neither is a major oil exporter and they both have access to the Mediterranean. However, the crisis has spurred a potential wider reconfiguration of regional trade and energy routes, as countries like Iraq look for alternatives. 

Both Beirut and Damascus have an opportunity to position their Mediterranean ports and transport networks as gateways between the Gulf and European markets in a reconfigured regional trading system.

Iraq–Syria pipeline

Iraq is already pursuing several ways to diversify its export routes. Baghdad is seeking to expand exports through Turkey’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, where Iraqi crude already flows, and is even discussing the revival of a long-stalled idea for a pipeline to Jordan’s Red Sea port of Aqaba.

Iraq and Syria are also pursuing a new pipeline that would carry Iraqi crude oil westwards to the Mediterranean. This would aim to give Baghdad another alternative to its overwhelming dependence on exports through the Strait of Hormuz. 

This planned corridor is often described as a revival of the historic Kirkuk–Baniyas pipeline, which once carried oil from northern Iraq to the Syrian coast. But it entails new infrastructure to form a wider network connecting Iraq’s southern and northern fields to a hub at Haditha in western Iraq, from which oil could flow west through Syria to the Mediterranean port of Baniyas and north towards Turkey.

Estimates put the cost at around $15 billion, with construction likely to take around four years. The Trump administration is reportedly supporting the plan as part of a strategy to reduce Iran’s regional leverage by diversifying away from Hormuz. 

The new network, which has a proposed initial capacity of around two million b/d, would allow Iraq to divert a substantial share of its exports away from Hormuz, reducing Iranian leverage. But it would diversify rather than replace Hormuz: most Iraqi crude exports go to Asian markets, particularly China and India, which are far quicker to reach from the Gulf than the Mediterranean.

New East–West corridors 

Lebanon and Syria are also exploring the restoration of railway links that could eventually connect the Lebanese coast through Syria to Iraq, Turkey and the Gulf. This month, Lebanese and Syrian officials inspected a potential rail route connecting the Lebanese port of Tripoli to Homs in Syria. This could be the potential first step in re-establishing Syria as a transit state, with Tripoli as a potential Mediterranean gateway.

Yet while rebuilding the short Tripoli-Homs railway may seem feasible, establishing a wider regional corridor will require much more infrastructure and faces challenges. Lebanon’s previous plans to revive the same railway stalled before work began, in part over financing and mismanagement. Syria’s railway system is badly damaged by war, with the government estimating that its rehabilitation could cost around $5.5 billion. 

The same pursuit of connectivity is extending into the digital realm. New fibre-optic networks through Iraq and Syria are intended to give Gulf states alternative land routes for the vast quantities of data that currently travel through vulnerable submarine cables.

Energy under attack

For now, there is a considerable gap between ambition and reality. Iraq, Syria and Lebanon are pursuing these infrastructure projects in the shadow of a war they cannot control and while facing external occupations or interference. 

In Lebanon, Israeli forces occupy a self-declared security zone in the south, with more than a million people displaced. In Syria, Israel seized the demilitarized buffer zone in December 2024 and has maintained a military presence there since. 

Across the Middle East, energy infrastructure has become a major target, with over 100 attacks on energy assets in the first six months of the war. Iran has attacked energy facilities across the Gulf, while Israel has struck fuel storage depots and gas infrastructure within Iran. 

Iran retains influence through its political and armed networks across the region. This includes groups embedded within Iraq and Lebanon that have repeatedly demonstrated their capacity to threaten critical infrastructure. 

Related work

The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea

In Iraq, for instance, the Khor Mor gas field has suffered repeated rocket and drone attacks blamed on militias. More recently, attacks launched from Iraqi territory forced the temporary closure of Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline, which is also designed to reduce Riyadh’s dependence on Hormuz. The Houthis have attacked Saudi oil tankers and seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait coastline this month.

The threat to infrastructure is not limited to Iran-aligned armed groups. Israel has repeatedly targeted transport infrastructure during the current conflict, including in Lebanon, demonstrating how the conflict can disrupt the physical networks on which greater connectivity would depend. And in eastern Syria, through which the proposed new Iraqi energy corridor would pass, armed groups including ISIS have attacked oil wells and tanker trucks.

Internal obstacles

Another obstacle is entrenched corruption. Iraq, Lebanon and Syria all sit near the bottom of Transparency International’s corruption perceptions index. 

In political systems where public contracting is a principal means of distributing rents, mega-projects can create opportunities for political parties to potentially profit from contracts, often at the expense of their delivery. 

Linked to this is the fragmentation of these states themselves. Infrastructure on this scale requires institutions capable of coordinating decisions over years, enforcing contracts, protecting assets and binding competing interests to a common project. 

Yet authority in Iraq, Syria and Lebanon remains fragmented among political factions, competing institutions and armed actors. This leaves governments unable to guarantee the security or financing of projects, with multiple actors able to obstruct their completion or extract rents. This creates a fundamental mismatch between the scale of ambition and the capacity to deliver it.

Connectivity doesn’t guarantee sovereignty 

The war has increased the strategic value of Iraq, Syria and Lebanon’s geographical position. As states and companies search for alternatives to Hormuz, the three countries offer potential alternative corridors connecting the Gulf to the Mediterranean and Europe.

Whether Iraq, Syria and Lebanon can take advantage of this opportunity will help determine whether they can shape the post-war regional order, or whether it is once again shaped around them. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

But connectivity is not the same as sovereignty. New pipelines, railways and trade corridors can offer these states alternatives to the dependencies of the old order, but alone they cannot produce sovereignty. That requires institutions capable of delivering and protecting these projects.

If Iraq, Syria and Lebanon want to seize the opportunities of the changing regional order, they will need to do more than build new routes across their borders. They will need to build states capable of governing these new connections, while ensuring that their benefits extend to their populations, not just elites.

title: ‘Coupling without fusion’: Canada and Europe test a new kind of alliance
author: jon.wallace
description:
‘Coupling without fusion’: Canada and Europe test a new kind of alliance Expert comment jon.wallace 18 September 2026

The deeper relationship proposed by Carney and von der Leyen could send a powerful geopolitical message. But can agreement be reached without antagonizing EU candidate countries? 

There is something rather extraordinary about the geopolitical times we live in. They are making what seemed impossible yesterday possible today, and what once sounded laughable increasingly credible. This week’s proposals for closer integration between Canada and the EU undoubtedly belongs to that category. 

On 16 September, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first ‘associate member’. The next day, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney used his address to the European Parliament to set out an unusually ambitious programme of economic and strategic integration. 

Canada and Europe, he argued, should cooperate across critical minerals, defence production, artificial intelligence and computing, energy, space and payments. They should move towards ‘seamless’ digital trade in non-agricultural goods and services. And they should expand opportunities for young Canadians and Europeans to live, work and study across the Atlantic. Canada also eyes access to the EU’s Horizon research programme.

If the concept of associate membership is yet to be properly defined – starting with meaningful legal substance – Carney’s address gave it discernible geopolitical purpose. His argument rests on a lesson he has repeated since his Davos speech in January 2026: excessive economic concentration creates vulnerability. And only diversification can restore room for political choice. In Carney’s own words in Strasbourg: ‘The objective is not self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience.’

That logic applies to both sides of the Atlantic. Canada remains extraordinarily exposed to the United States (US), which takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports. The EU has its own dependencies – including on US technology and security capabilities, Chinese supply chains and, of course, energy imports. 

In this context, both sides of the Atlantic see partnership as a timely opportunity. Seen from Brussels, Canada has much to offer: energy, minerals, Arctic reach, investment capital and advanced capabilities in areas including AI, quantum and space. Seen from Ottawa, the EU also brings a lot to the table: a single market of 450 million consumers, a still strong industrial capacity, world-class research networks and considerable regulatory power.

Want to hear more on the national and economic security intersection in competition policy?

Join us at our competition policy conference to explore how competition policy frameworks are responding to changes in the geopolitical order.

This momentum did not suddenly emerge this week. But the Carney and von der Leyen speeches moved the conversation a step further, giving stronger political expression to a relationship that has been deepening for some time. In June, for instance, Canada became the first non-European country formally brought into procurement under the EU’s €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence instrument.  

The relationship is clearly strengthening well beyond trade. It now connects industrial policy, defence production, technology and economic security in ways that the EU has rarely attempted with a non-European power, Japan being probably the closest precedent.

A transatlantic hedge more than a new bloc

Donald Trump’s swift reaction indicates the extent to which the notion of Canadian associate membership really matters. The US president described the prospect as potentially a ‘hostile act’ and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if Washington concluded that the initiative was directed against the US. Carney responded that Canada would determine its own international partnerships. 

Yet Carney was equally explicit that he is not seeking to construct a rival geopolitical bloc. His proposal might be better understood as an attempt to give countries exposed to great-power economic pressure greater freedom of action. In a way, this model resembles what architects would call ‘coupling without fusion’: two structures that reinforce one another against external pressure but retain their own foundations. 

Canada cannot realistically detach its economy from that of the US. Nor can Europe dispense with the transatlantic security relationship at this stage: the recent trip of the German defence minister to Washington would even indicate the opposite. The purpose here is to reduce specific dependencies on partners like the US while remaining allies.

If it works, the implications could extend well beyond Canada. Von der Leyen has separately proposed a European Security Council involving partners including Canada, Britain, Norway and Ukraine. Carney himself described the Canada–EU arrangement as potentially open to other democracies. All those ideas point towards a looser outer architecture around the EU, where countries participate selectively in European structures without becoming member states. 

In this configuration, the EU would remain the constitutional core of a wider system of concentric circles. Associated countries would be integrated into selected markets, programmes and security structures without acquiring the political rights reserved for members. 

The law has yet to catch up with the politics

Nevertheless, at this stage the ‘associate member’ status remains a political expression rather than a legal category. Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union says that any European state may apply for EU membership. Canada does not meet that geographical requirement.

Creating a formal new category of membership with institutional rights – representation in EU bodies, for example – would therefore require treaty revision. Under Article 48, amendments ultimately require ratification by every member state according to its procedures. That makes genuine constitutional ‘associate membership’ a very ambitious undertaking.

There is, however, an easier route. Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU does permit agreements with third countries establishing an association based on reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedures. Such association agreements require unanimity in the Council and the consent of the European Parliament. Brussels and Ottawa could therefore deliver most of what Carney envisages without embarking on the long and painstaking journey of treaty revision.

Politically, such an option could suit Canada better. Carney stressed after his speech that sovereignty would be preserved and that any final arrangement would be put to a vote in Canada. He also played down the importance of what Brussels eventually calls it. The difficult negotiations would concern regulatory alignment, market access and reciprocal obligations rather than the ‘nomenclature’.

In Canada, opposition is already visible. Pierre Poilievre’s Conservatives support trade and defence links with Europe but have warned against EU taxation, legislation or free-movement rules applying to Canada. And they argue that Parliament must scrutinize any transfer of authority. 

In Europe, diplomats have questioned what associate membership would mean and noted that von der Leyen’s proposal had not been agreed with the member states beforehand. EU candidate countries could also reasonably ask why Canada should receive privileged access while they undergo years of regulatory and political reform to qualify for membership.

But the immediate warning sign is more tangible. Ten EU member states – including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland – have still not ratified the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), nine years after its provisional application began. That unfinished business points towards the political challenges ahead. How likely are EU member states to reach agreement on Canada’s associate membership when a simple free trade agreement struggles to secure full ratification? 

CETA would be the best framework available to provide the commercial foundation of a new Canada–EU association. Defence cooperation through SAFE already offers a template for selective participation in EU instruments. Negotiations would now need to proceed on digital trade, research, student and youth mobility, critical minerals and energy. Institutional arrangements would then gradually build around them.

To borrow an apocryphal line from Lenin, there are decades when nothing happens and weeks when decades happen. These past few days in Strasbourg may come to be remembered as one of those moments when history accelerates.

The EU and Canada are testing how far integration can be achieved between countries that want greater strategic independence without merging their political institutions. Success could have implications far beyond the Atlantic. One conclusion can already be drawn, however: another kind of transatlantic relationship is possible.

title: Turkish central bank resumes rate cuts and signals more to come
description: TURKEY: The Turkish central bank has cut the policy rate by 100bp to 36%, as expected, amid improving inflation and continued weakness in domestic demand. The bank also indicated that additional rate cuts are likely unless there is a material shift in the conditions underpinning the current rate-cutting cycle

title: The Dutch economy is doing surprisingly well
description: EUROPE: The Dutch economy continues to grow at a decent pace despite persistent inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and domestic capacity constraints. Strong household spending has helped so far, but the growth engine is gradually shifting towards exports and investment

title: Polish consumers keep spending, but momentum softens
description: Retail sales were slightly weaker, but not disappointing. This can be explained by the absence of the fuel discount programme (CPN) in September and slowing real wage growth. On the other hand, sales of durable goods continue to grow at a solid pace

title: Heatwaves have exposed a blind spot in Belgium’s housing stock
description: BELGIUM: Nearly nine in 10 Belgians say their home was uncomfortably hot in 2026, exposing a blind spot in the renovation debate: energy efficiency alone does not guarantee summer comfort. Belgium therefore faces a dual renovation challenge of cutting energy use while adapting homes to a warmer climate

title: French business confidence defies the turmoil for now
description: EUROPE: October’s unexpected rebound in business confidence is good news, particularly for industry. But the survey does not yet capture the impact of the latest social unrest, while higher interest rates, a weak labour market and deteriorating public finances are clouding the outlook further

title: Webinar: Directional Economics – Central Europe’s new horizons, from investment hosts to global investors
description: CENTRAL AND EASTERN EUROPE: The CEE region has been hit hard by a further energy shock. Yet despite the challenging macroeconomic environment, much of the region has shown great resilience. Join ING's team of experts for a live webinar on 29 October to hear more about the next phase of economic convergence, outward investment, and the fiscal and monetary policy outlook

title: FX Daily: Defensive rotation in play
description: It looks like markets are going through a subtle regime shift. Higher energy prices no longer mean higher rates forever; instead, the long end is starting to express a little more fear about growth. The upcoming US midterms may also be playing a role. It looks like there is some defensive rotation underway into the Swiss franc, the yen and sterling

title: ECB caught in the French drama
description: EUROPE: The European Central Bank meeting on 29 October is not expected to result in an interest rate hike. Instead, the French crisis is increasingly eroding the need for additional rate hikes

title: The Commodities Feed: Attacks on Saudi Arabia fan oil supply worries
description: Oil prices remain well-supported after fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia, with traders focused on risks to the outlook rather than the resilience of Persian Gulf supplies
